findings.title: Refunds are marked complete without the provider reconciliation the docs promise
findings.description: docs/payments.md says refunds are accepted (202) and reconciled with the provider in the daily settlement run, but nothing in this change calls a payment provider: `refund()` only writes local rows and a locally generated `reference` token, and `SettlementService.settleBatchAtomic` only inserts ledger rows for captured payments. As a result the internal state says refunded while the customer's funds have not been returned, and the `refunds.reference` column stores a local random token rather than a provider reference.

evidence.snippet: Refunds are accepted immediately (`202 Accepted`) and reconciled with the provider in the daily
evidence.note: The documented contract requires provider reconciliation.
The reference persisted and returned is generated locally, not obtained from a provider.
The refund is recorded as final locally with no provider call and no pending/outbox state.

findings.whyItMatters: Customers can be told a refund was accepted while no money is ever returned; the reconciliation step claimed by the documentation does not exist in the settlement path, so nothing will detect the missing provider refund.
consequences: Payment marked refunded locally with the customer's funds never released
No pending/failed state that a retry or reconciliation job could pick up
findings.reproduction: Call the refund endpoint and grep the settlement path for any provider call — none exists, so the locally recorded refund is never transmitted.
findings.recommendation: Either perform synchronously (or enqueue) the provider refund call and store the provider reference, or add a persisted `pending_provider` state plus the reconciliation step in `settleBatchAtomic`, and update docs/payments.md to match what the code actually does.

findings.title: 'atomic' settlement result advertises a guarantee the repository transaction boundary does not provide
findings.description: settleBatchAtomic now documents and returns `atomic: true`, but the only implementation of the boundary it relies on, PostgresPaymentRepository.withTransaction, simply invokes the callback against the same repository (`return work(this)`) and never begins, commits or rolls back anything. The settlement code therefore reports success in the language of a transaction while a failure halfway through the loop still leaves earlier ledger inserts committed.

evidence.snippet: * The batch is settled inside a transaction so a failure half way through
evidence.note: The comment states the isolation property the code depends on.
The withTransaction implementation runs the work with no BEGIN/COMMIT and no rollback path.

findings.whyItMatters: The abstraction is now present and trusted in the domain layer but is a pass-through in its only implementation; the failure mode it promises to prevent (ledger ahead of the batch) is still possible, and the `atomic` flag makes callers believe otherwise.
consequences: A ledger insert failing on row N leaves rows 1..N-1 committed while the caller sees a rejected promise and a RetrySettlement rebuilds duplicate ledger rows.
Consumers of SettlementResult.atomic treat the batch as consistent and skip a reconciliation check.
findings.recommendation: Either implement withTransaction against a pooled client (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK on a dedicated connection) before returning `atomic: true`, or do not return the atomic flag until the repository honours it — and add a test that forces a mid-loop failure and asserts no ledger rows remain.
